title: CHAPTER NINETEEN. On Gods blessedness; definition
english: Thus far was the integrity of Gods life, which stands as virtue: there follows that which stands as blessedness, and it is the act of Gods life by which He so enjoys His infinite perfection fully known through the intellect and supremely loved through His will that He wholly rests in it.
All who confess that God is, throughout the whole world, call God most blessed. Thing His blessedness consists, many doubt, reasoning about His    blessedness from our satiated appetites.

title: Against placing blessedness in power, external wisdom, or pleasure alone
english: The Machiavellians of our time place blessedness in dominion alone. But they err (1) who constitute it in power and dominion alone, or in conservation of oneself by resisting power long in that. For horse and lion are more powerful than man, who yet rules them by wisdom; and a strong man without wisdom is not conserved, and tyrants themselves are of all the most unhappy. Thus a stone would be more blessed than an eagle or a man.

(2) Nor does it consist in wisdom of external things, because that comes about in us not without prior passion; and the wise man, if powerless, is exposed to many miseries, nor is he preserved by his wisdom if he is not good; and though he be best to himself, yet if he considers something better in another, he does not think himself blessed but becomes wretched by envy.

(3) Nor in the sole full enjoyment of pleasures of love. For who enjoys while ignorant and does not taste the enjoyment, nor can conserve himself in it — who will be blessed? Better is he who knows how to abound and to suffer want than he who abounds without sense. (4) Love of self also falls short of blessedness when something better is seen elsewhere, or what is loved cannot be made eternal. Therefore all who think blessedness consists in power alone or wisdom alone or love alone or any other private good err.

title: Boethius; blessedness as essential identity with God; power, wisdom, love
english: More rightly Boethius defines the state as perfect by aggregation of all goods, which yet in God are not aggregated but are essentially one, since He can, knows, and loves all things, and so is Himself sufficient to Himself.

If you ask in which of these three perfections blessedness chiefly consists: you will not easily say in any one, but equally in the three. Yet if one ought to be judged more potent, love will be more potent, whose object is the good which formally blesses; but as known it is not the good. Love presupposes power and wisdom, and so as it were completes essence and blessedness.

Power does not suppose wisdom and love: but wisdom precedes love and is as it were ordered to it, although not formally but radically all blessedness is in power and likewise in wisdom and love. It begins as it were in power, proceeds through wisdom, is consummated in love.

title: Objection: hatred of sins and things God cannot undo; reply — essential beatitude
english: But you will say: if God is blessed because He can, knows, and loves all things, He seems not perfectly blessed, because He holds many things in hatred, as sins, and many escape His power, because He cannot make what is done undone.

Reply: Gods blessedness is God Himself, the adequate object of His love, and of wisdom and power. For blessedness is not from outside and accidental to Him, as Bernard puts it, but for God to be and to be blessed are the same. Hence the being all things, and the knowledge of Himself which is at once of all things, make Gods blessedness.

But to be able outwardly, as regards active or passive power, and likewise to know and love exterior things, is not essential blessedness but a flight from and remedy of need, as in us who love food, wife, honor, by which we are conserved because we cannot be conserved in ourselves and through ourselves. Therefore in us to be and to be blessed are not the same. But God is not so, since the infinity of His perfections is without beginning of deficiency and need, and their object is the same as they themselves. It can be said that God outwardly can all things, knows all things, and loves all things, while in Himself He can be what He is, and knows Himself and loves Himself. For all things participate His likeness. But God is said not to be able and not to know and not to will certain things which are not truly beings — sins, contradictions, privations — concerning which it is certain that to be able, know, and love those does not hang on power, wisdom, and love, but on impotence, folly, and, so to speak, dislike, or a share of these.

title: Essential property; creatures beatific good; glory
english: But Gods blessedness is an essential property, indeed the essence itself, which can be communicated to no creature — Isaiah 42:8; Jeremiah; 1 Corinthians 15:28; 1 Timothy 1:11; 6:15; Psalm 16:2,11. And yet it is the beatific good of intelligent creatures by reason of the object completing the act tending into the object and resting in the same, in which two the creatures blessedness consists and shines. For the object is the good which we enjoy. But the act is that by which we enjoy the good.

And it is glory or joy. III. Glory is that by which, on account of His infinite perfection, He excels all things. And so this attribute is indeed from Gods perfection, but with a certain respect outwardly, because He variously manifests His excellence above all things and His infinite perfection by external acts — Romans 1:23; 9:5; Psalm 8; Deuteronomy 32; 1 Timothy 1:11; 6:15.

And that either through unusual flashing and shining of light and splendor, or through opposed and split darkness, or through production of works which agree with His perfection and excellence — Matthew 17:2,5; Luke 2:9; Exodus; Psalm 19:1.

title: God objectively and effectively the blessedness of all; joy — Cap. 19 COMPLETE
english: It is manifest that God is not only His own blessedness objectively and formally, but also of all things objectively and effectively. For all things are blessed in some measure by some good, and especially intelligent creatures; but God is the efficient and exemplar cause of every good, and every good is a certain participation of Him. There are indeed those who think God is also formally the creatures blessedness, because He is more intrinsic to things than their own act: but they err. For God is indeed in us, yet not some part of essence or our whole essence formally, but only causally and eminently.

And if indeed the highest good for each is its own being and conservation: yet because they neither are nor are conserved from themselves but from God: therefore they are also blessed by Him, and love Him more than themselves while they love themselves. For they love not only what they are, but would wish to be that always and everywhere and seek extensive and intensive infinity, which is in God alone, in whom there is never or anywhere any defect of goodness — which blessedness is called eternal life, which God does not acquire from elsewhere by His virtues, but by them gives it to others.

IV. Joy is that by which He pleasantly enjoys Himself. This is not a variable affection. For God is affected with perfect joy and perpetually delights in Himself, to use Lactantius word — Zephaniah 3:17. If you ask a philosopher concerning Gods blessedness, Aristotle of Stagira in On the Heavens book 1 chapter 9 attributes to God a life most sufficient to Himself. Nothing truer than this saying was brought forth by this pagan. CHAPTER TWENTY, On Gods figurative attributes, follows.
